### Study design

We aimed to estimate the effect of model structure on forecast performance.
We evaluated weekly forecasts of COVID-19 outcomes of incident cases and deaths, for 32 European countries between 8 March 2021 and 10 March 2023, collected by the public European COVID-19 Forecast Hub [@euroHub2021].
The Hub solicited real-time forecasts one to four weeks ahead.
Any forecaster was eligible for inclusion, with no selection criteria.
For this analysis, we excluded forecasts that did not report the full set of 23 quantiles or that were more than four weeks ahead.
Models could forecast any subset of the four horizons, noting that 8 of 48 did not forecast all four.
We also excluded the ensemble of all Hubs models.
Full eligibility and a STROBE flow diagram are given in the Supplement.

We evaluated forecasts against Johns Hopkins University data on cumulative daily reported cases and deaths [@dong2020], converted to incident weekly counts, as available on 10 March 2023 when collation stopped.
Before evaluation, we normalised forecasts and observations to incidence per 100,000 population and log-transformed both.
This supports comparability across varying populations with varying magnitude of incidence across locations and over time.
The log-transform can also be read as evaluating prediction of the growth rate [@bosse2023].

We scored forecasts with the weighted interval score (WIS), a proper scoring rule and generalisation of the continuous ranked probability score, reflecting a forecast's dispersion, overprediction and underprediction [@bracher2021].
We report this log-transformed data evaluated with the WIS as the LWIS, and separately report the natural-scale WIS in the Supplement.

#### Forecasting processes

We classified model structures as "Agent-based" (detailed individual-level interactions), "Mechanistic" (broadly compartmental), "Semi-mechanistic" (statistical models with epidemiological elements such as delay distributions or generation intervals), "Statistical" (context-agnostic time-series), and "Judgement" (ensembles of human-judgement predictions).
Classification used self-reported metadata, which included an optional description of methods, and links to model code, website or publication (schema and example in the Supplement).
Four authors (KS, SF, FB, JM) classified models independently, with at least two rating each model.
The majority vote determined the final classification, ties were resolved by an additional independent rater, and two investigators (SF, KS) reviewed all classifications.

We classified each model as forecasting for a single country, or for more than one (noting that forecasters changed the number of targets they submitted over time).
We included the length of forecast horizon to represent increasing uncertainty of forecasting further ahead.
We included this as both an effect shared by all models, and also allowed for a per-model variation (as each model's penalised deviation from the shared horizon effect, including the overall level of each model).
This per-model term also separates the contribution of model structure from variation between individual models.

#### Target processes

We included the epidemiological outcome of incident cases or deaths as a fixed effect acting on forecast scores.
We then allowed the effect of model structure to differ between outcomes.
We also included a random effect for target country, to account for residual population-level epidemic variation.
We then considered observable time-varying factors associated with transmission dynamics.
We included the count of incident outcomes; the trend of incidence ("Stable", "Increasing" or "Decreasing", from a three-week moving average, with a change of +/-5% as "Stable"); and the dominant pathogen variant in the target country (classified from public viral sequencing data into discrete variant phases [@variant-data]).

We considered whether these time-varying factors (incidence, trend and variant phase) should be considered prospectively, from the forecaster's perspective, or retrospectively, from the perspective of the target outcome.
Here, we included covariates in the week ending eight days before the forecast date, using finalised counts.
This accounted for information available to forecasters as they produced predictions.
We conservatively used the most recent week likely to have been fully reported.
Alternatively, we considered using covariates as observed at the target date.
This would help demonstrate the difficulty of a target in retrospect.
However, conditioning on values that were not available in the forecaster's information set would weight scores by realised outcomes, therefore biasing an evaluation of forecaster accuracy independent of that outcome (analogous to the "forecaster's dilemma" [@lerch2017]).
We intended to account for prospective, predictable difficulty shared among forecasters, therefore we included covariates as known before the forecast date.
We report the alternative view referenced to the target date in the Supplement.

#### Residual confounding

We did not adjust for unobserved characteristics of the forecasting team, such as capacity, infrastructure, or experience, although these plausibly shape both the choice of model structure and realised performance.
-->

### Model-based analysis

We assessed the direct effect of model structure on WIS.
We illustrate our approach with a directed acyclic graph (Supplement).

```{r}
#| label: methods-setup
#| include: false

library(here)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
# Tweedie power parameter of the primary fit, so the text tracks the fit
tweedie_p <- read_csv(here("output", "diagnostics", "fit-summary.csv"),
                      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(spec_label == "forecast-lag1", scale == "log") |>
  pull(family) |>
  (\(x) as.numeric(sub(".*p=([0-9.]+).*", "\\1", x)))()
```

We fitted a single hierarchical model across both epidemiological outcomes.
The LWIS is continuous, non-negative and strongly right-skewed, so we treated the LWIS of each forecast $i$ as Tweedie-distributed with a log link, letting the linear predictor $\eta_i$ act multiplicatively on the expected score:

$$
  \mathrm{LWIS}_i \sim \mathrm{Tw}_p(\mu_i,\, \phi), \qquad \log \mu_i = \eta_i,
$$

where $\phi$ is the dispersion and the power parameter $p \in (1, 2)$ is estimated alongside the smoothing parameters, giving a variance function $\mathrm{Var}(\mathrm{LWIS}_i) = \phi\,\mu_i^{p}$.
We adopted a Tweedie distribution to support forecasts scoring exactly zero.
We compared this against a Gaussian and a Gamma on the same specification (see Supplement).
The estimated $p$ was `r round(tweedie_p, 2)`, close to a Gamma, but a Gamma has no support at zero and would require an arbitrary constant for these scores.

The linear predictor decomposed into a fixed intercept, a fixed effect for the epidemiological outcome, random-effect contributions from categorical covariates, and two smooths for continuous covariates:

$$
  \eta_i
  = \beta_0 \; + \; \beta_{\text{outcome}}\,\mathbb{1}[\text{Deaths}_i] \;
    + \; \underbrace{\sum_{g \in \mathcal{G}} u^{g}_{j_g(i)}}_{\text{random effects}} \;
    + \; \underbrace{f_{\text{Inc}}(\mathrm{Incidence}_i) \;+\; f_{\text{Horizon}}(\mathrm{Horizon}_i) \;+\; f^{\text{Horizon}}_{k(i)}(\mathrm{Horizon}_i)}_{\text{smooths}}.
$$

Here $\beta_{\text{outcome}}$ gives the deaths-versus-cases contrast on the log scale (cases as reference) and is not part of the zero-mean Gaussian random-effects set $\mathcal{G}$, and $j_g(i)$ denotes the level of grouping factor $g$ for forecast $i$:

$$
  u^{g}_{j} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, \sigma^2_g), \qquad g
  \in \mathcal{G}
  = \{\text{Method} \times \text{Outcome},\, \text{CountryTargets},\, \text{Trend},\, \text{Variant},\, \text{Location}\}.
$$

Model structure enters as a single grouping factor crossing with epidemiological outcome, giving one effect per cell, so a structure may predict cases relatively better than deaths or the reverse.
We report both the separate effects per outcome and the pooled effect of each structure as a contrast averaging its two cells, which accounts for the covariance between them.
The epidemiological outcome remains a fixed effect.
Being unpenalised, this absorbs any difference common to all structures, leaving the crossed term to carry variation from it.
Both choices are set out in the Supplement.

$f_{\text{Inc}}$ was a penalised thin-plate regression spline over log-transformed incidence.
Forecast performance is known to worsen with horizon, so $f_{\text{Horizon}}$ was a smooth of horizon shared by all models.
Each model $k$ had its own deviation from this curve, $f^{\text{Horizon}}_k$, with its level and slope penalised towards zero.
Both smooths used four basis functions.
We compare alternative horizon specifications in the Supplement.

We fitted all models with the `mgcv` package in R using fast restricted maximum likelihood [@wood2011].
We checked fit by visual inspection of residuals and conducted extensive sensitivity analysis.
To assess confounding, we also fitted univariate models to provide a comparison between unadjusted and adjusted estimates of the effect of model structure on LWIS.
We report each categorical effect as the exponentiated random effect, which multiplies the expected LWIS relative to the population mean (a zero random effect), with all other terms held fixed; the epidemiological outcome is reported as deaths relative to cases.
A ratio of 0.9 represents an expected LWIS 10% lower (better) than the population mean.
We report each individual model's effect as its average deviation from the shared horizon curve over the horizons for which that model forecast.
We report raw partial effects in the Supplement.

All data and code are publicly available online [@sherratt2025].
